Using strat_data, which contains only strategy users determined from the 95% CI criteria, we can fit an exponential, single-step, two-step model to their aiming data and see which model fits best via AIC. 

# ONE STEP
 mean2 <- par["mean2"] – mean of step size 
  <br>trial1 <-  trial that step happens. (gamma?)
  <br>sd2   <- par["sd2"]. -  variation of steps people take with rotation. 
  <br>sd1   <- par["sd1"] -   variation of aims during baseline
  
```{r}
fit_onestep_model()
```


# TWO-STEP
  mean2 <- par["mean2"] – mean of step size 
  <br>mean3 <- par["mean2"] – mean of second step size 
 <br> trial1 <-  trial that step happens. (gamma?)
 <br> trial2 <-  trial that second step happens. (gamma?)
 <br> sd2   <- par["sd2"]. -  variation of steps people take with rotation. 
 <br> sd1   <- par["sd1"] -   variation of aims during baseline
```{r}
 fit_twostep_model()
```


# EXPONENTIAL
N0 
<br>Lambda. 

```{r}
fit_exponential_model()
```



## Steps.
### 1.	Take last 8 baseline trials and first 50 rotated. At trial = 0 is where the rotation gets introduced.

### 2.	 Fit each model through each participant
a.	Step:  when a participant changes their aim deviation (>=15 degrees) at trial X and keeps their aim above or equal to 15 degrees
b.	Two-step:  participants make a smaller aim change (>=6 degrees) at trial X but then in the next few trials increases their aim (>=15 degrees)
c.	Exponential decay function: participants adjust their aim (>=15 degrees) gradually (say every 1-2 degrees) over multiple trials.  

### 3.	Calculate mse per each participant

### 4.	Store aic values for each participant expAIC <- Reach::AIC(mse, 2, n)

```{r}
  compute_aic <- function(mse, k, n) {
    Reach::AIC(mse, k, n)
  }  

  step1_aic <- compute_aic(step1_fit$mse, step1_fit$k, n_trials)
  step2_aic <- compute_aic(step2_fit$mse, step2_fit$k, n_trials)
  exp_aic   <- compute_aic(exp_fit$mse, exp_fit$k, n_trials)
  
```

### 5.	For each participant, compare aic values from each model… smallest one wins!
